rationale: B wins by discipline, not sparkle: its line "the IPO context extends it only if there is a filing or a date, and there is neither" is the kind of guardrail that keeps a founder out of trouble. A has strong shapes, but "Why would a company chasing an IPO give away its flagship AI model?" overcooks two facts at once: no IPO date and no supplied proof this is the flagship or core monetizable IP. A gives more doors to knock on; B tells you which ones will not embarrass you when opened.
gaps_in_A: "flagship AI model" is not in the update. The facts say a new foundation model, not flagship, core, or necessarily monetizable IP.
"company chasing an IPO" loads the dice. The update says Databricks has signaled an eventual IPO without a date; A later questions that, but the headline already oversells it.
The IPO angle asks for valuation and signal proof, but misses the first markets-reporter question: how "annualized revenue" is calculated and what the prior-year comparison actually was.

"Today's release adds a new entrant/data point to an active industry debate" relies on broad industry context that was not supplied. It is plausible, but it should be framed as a testable context claim, not a given.
gaps_in_B: "buyers who cannot send data outside their own environment" is an inference, not a supplied fact. It may be true for some regulated buyers, but the angle needs a customer or compliance source before saying it flatly.

B collapses the regulated-buyer story and the closed-API competitive story into "Databricks takes aim at closed AI APIs with an open model for regulated buyers." That is efficient, but it leaves a cleaner compliance/procurement category angle on the table.
"giving its foundation model away" is punchy but still depends on the license. B catches this in proof, but the headline should not outrun the exact license terms.
